metadata.name: [GCP Cloud SQL SQL Server OTel] CPU saturated with runnable task queue
metadata.description: Alerts when the average CPU utilization of a SQL Server instance is at or above 90% of its reserved vCPUs over 15 minutes and, at the same time, the SQL Server scheduler run queue (runnable_tasks summed across schedulers) averages at least 1 task, for 3 consecutive checks. High CPU with an empty run queue is a busy but healthy server and does not fire. Requires at least 5 minutes of samples and applies the SQL Server engine marker. Grouped by database_id.

query.base:
TS metrics-gcp.cloudsql_sqlserver.otel-*
| WHERE gcp.resource_type == "cloudsql_database"
// Per minute: exact CPU sums across fragments, and the instance run queue
// (runnable_tasks has one series per scheduler_id; one sample per series per minute).
| STATS cpu_sum = SUM(SUM_OVER_TIME(`cloudsql.googleapis.com/database/cpu/utilization`)),
        cpu_n = SUM(COUNT_OVER_TIME(`cloudsql.googleapis.com/database/cpu/utilization`)),
        cpu_peak = MAX(MAX_OVER_TIME(`cloudsql.googleapis.com/database/cpu/utilization`)),
        run_queue = SUM(SUM_OVER_TIME(`cloudsql.googleapis.com/database/sqlserver/schedulers/runnable_tasks`)),
        rq_n = SUM(COUNT_OVER_TIME(`cloudsql.googleapis.com/database/sqlserver/schedulers/runnable_tasks`)),
        cores = MAX(MAX_OVER_TIME(`cloudsql.googleapis.com/database/cpu/reserved_cores`)),
        ss = SUM(COUNT_OVER_TIME(`cloudsql.googleapis.com/database/sqlserver/memory/page_life_expectancy`))
    BY `@timestamp` = TBUCKET(1 minute), database_id
// Ignore minutes without scheduler samples instead of counting them as an empty queue
| EVAL run_queue = CASE(rq_n > 0, run_queue, NULL)
| STATS cpu_sum = SUM(cpu_sum), cpu_n = SUM(cpu_n), cpu_peak = MAX(cpu_peak),
        rq_avg = AVG(run_queue), rq_peak = MAX(run_queue),
        cores = MAX(cores), ss = SUM(ss)
    BY database_id

data.content:
## Cloud SQL for SQL Server CPU saturated

The instance used at least 90% of its reserved vCPUs on average over 15 minutes, and SQL Server's schedulers had runnable tasks queued (`rq_avg`), so queries are waiting for CPU. Every query slows down.

### Triage
1. Open the Instance Detail dashboard: compare CPU, runnable tasks, batch requests and login attempts. Did traffic rise (more batches) or did per-query cost rise (same batches, more CPU)?
2. A login spike with flat batches points to a connection storm (poor pooling); authentication consumes CPU.
3. Memory pressure (falling page life expectancy, rising read IOPS) often precedes CPU rises; check the memory pressure alert.
4. Use Query Insights / `sys.dm_exec_query_stats` to find the top CPU consumers; look for plan regressions or missing indexes.
5. If load is legitimate, scale the tier (more vCPUs).

### Tuning
- `cpu_avg_pct >= 90`: CPU threshold. Lower to 80 for earlier warning.
- `rq_avg >= 1`: run-queue threshold. Remove the line to alert on CPU utilization alone, or raise it on large instances (e.g. to `cores`).

### Behaviour notes
- Healthy: average CPU below 90%, or high CPU with an average run queue below 1. Breaching: both CPU >= 90% and run queue >= 1 (equality breaches), for 3 consecutive checks (about 25 minutes sustained).
- Missing data: instances with fewer than 5 CPU samples or no scheduler samples in the window are not evaluated.
